analysis.title: US EQUITIES - less risk appetite
key_insights: GS's Risk Appetite Indicator (RAI) posted the largest monthly drop in global risk appetite since November 2021. The level is still not low enough to signal the contrarian buying opportunities of recent years, because the starting point was high.
After the 11 largest RAI declines since 2005, S&P outcomes ranged from -17% to +7% over 1 month and -32% to +18% over 6 months, so tail risk runs in both directions.
Hedge funds had a hard October. Fundamental L/S lost 3.5% and systematic L/S lost 3.6%, including a 2.5% loss last week, the worst since December 2023.

Positioning is mixed. Gross exposure is 314% (97th percentile over 5 years) while net exposure is in the 10th percentile over 1 year. Fundamental L/S beta-adjusted net fell to a 1-year low. Managers keep cutting market exposure but leverage stays high, which leaves fuel for more volatility.
Institutions remain short VIX futures but have covered aggressively over the last couple of weeks, nearly matching the covering seen in Q1.

Aggregate earnings are not the problem. With 60% of the S&P reported, EPS growth is tracking +33% y/y and 70% of stocks have risen since earnings season began. The weakness is in the largest, best-owned names, especially hyperscalers, where strong results did not clear a higher bar.

The AI debate is shifting from growth to the cost and financing of that growth. Hyperscaler capex is expected to reach $1.2tn in 2027, aggregate FCF turned negative in Q3, and upward earnings revisions are moderating, all in crowded and heavily levered parts of the market.

A GS Research note argues the AI funding gap may be smaller than feared. Oracle plans to spend about $220bn on AI infrastructure but expects to raise just $20bn through 2030, and GS Credit estimates the bond market could absorb another ~$500bn of hyperscaler debt.

On AI demand, the next wave is expected to come from companies using AI across everyday businesses rather than just coding. Microsoft's AI development platform is growing +300% y/y, and the open question is now who makes money from it.

AI-related equity volatility has overtaken energy as a key driver of bond yields. Investors are still underweight Treasuries, so yields have room to fall further if risk-off continues. The Fed was close to a sideshow this week, with Warsh striking a measured tone and GIR still expecting another hike in December.

Midterms are next week. Democrats are now over 90% likely to take the House, and GIR sees limited immediate market effect. Higher tariffs (about 2pts on the effective rate) and the Dec 11 funding deadline are the bigger risks, while data center regulatory crackdown fears look overdone.

The desk sees reasons for a more constructive near-term stance given earnings resilience and a considerable positioning reset. Elevated gross leverage and the unresolved AI debate leave room for further volatility.
